TENDELE: ACTIVISTS AT RISK

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A coal-mine pushing excavation in an environmentally sensitive area. An activist gunned down. We visit a community divided northern KZN as tension mounts.

Unique Selling Point:
NEWSY - INSIGHT INTO BREWING ISSUE - ACTIVISTS KILLED IN COLD BLOOD - A COMMUNITY DIVIDED WHILE A MINING OPERATION PUSHES AHEAD.

Summary:
Carte Blanche visits this community that has been divided by the Somkhele Mine Operations. Families opposing the move live in fear. Blood has drawn, lives lost. 63 year old Fikile Ntshangase was gunned down in her homestead in October, she fiercely opposed the the expansion of the mining development and was taken out in cold blood.
We ask what will it take to bring peace and harmony back to Ophondweni.


Further information:
Plans for the expansion of operations at the Somkhele mine on the border of the Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Park has brought strife to the community and the mine’s owner, Tendele Coal, is now taking legal steps to forcefully relocate residents of 24 homes in Ophondweni and Emalahleni villages under the Mpukunyoni Traditional Council (MTC).
Somkhele mine, owned and operated by Tendele Coal (Pty) Ltd, is one of the country’s largest suppliers of anthracite. The Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation (MCEJO) currently has two other court cases (one in the Supreme Court of Appeal and another in the North Gauteng High Court) against Tendele Coal, the Minister of Mineral Resources and Energy and nine others. Both those cases challenge Tendele’s operations.
Fikile Ntshangase, 63, was shot dead on October 22 in Ophondweni, KwaZulu-Natal, metres away from her 13-year-old grandson and his two friends, aged eight and 10, while she sat chopping onions for supper.
She was the deputy chairperson of the Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation (Mcejo), which had resolutely fought against the expansion of Tendele Coal Mining’s operations near the border of the Hluhluwe-Imfolozi Game Reserve.
Mcejo’s opposition has fractured the community, with a spate of violence that began in April this year when 19 bullets rained on the home of another anti-mining activist, Tholakele Mthethwa, leading to the October 22 killing of Ntshangase.
The community has been fighting for years to keep the lush beauty of the area pristine, but others desperately need work from the mine and its expansion.
What was once an ordinary village in which community members herded cattle and ploughed their fields has turned into a Wild West. Men walk around with revolvers holstered to their sides in the area in which they grew up and raised their families.
In November, The Global Environmental Trust, joined by the Centre for Environmental Rights and Mcejo, appeared in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein to try to overturn the 2018 Pietermaritzburg high court ruling that refused to interdict the expansion of Tendele’s operations, which currently cover more than 22 000 hectares.
Judgment in the appeal has been reserved.
We speak to the affected community members, their legal counsel, the commity and Conservationist Bobby Peek – about the impact, the challenges and the way forward in wa world where activists are increasingly in the firing line.

Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: In December 2020, Fikile Ntshangase was recognised as the Human Rights Defender of the year. She was not there to collect the award because she was gunned down at her homestead in rural KZN.

She fiercely opposed the expansion of mining operations in her local village.

BLAST UPSOUND

Often these operations come with the promise of economic growth and social development.

LINK: BUT it also brought friction, intimidation and murder to a community in northern KwaZulu Natal that’s been divided by the prospect of a vast anthracite mine expansion.

VO: The Somkhele mine, operated by Tendele Coal, a subsidiary of Petmin – is one of the country’s largest suppliers of anthracite.

The mine started in 2007 close to the Mfolozi-Hluhluwe Park in northern KZN. If it is to continue with the operation - it needs to expand. And 145 families need to make way.

THABO: All of us are forced, we were not given an option to decide so somebody or people have taken the decision for us.

VO: This man is from one of the 16 families yet to finalise relocation negotiations with the mine.

But as pressure to move mounts, threats increase and fear grows. He has asked us to hide his identity – it is his voice, but the visuals are of an actor.

THABO: I fear for my life and for my family and also for the community that I am with.

VO: Kirsten Youens is legal council for the Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation known as MCEJO – the organisation is challenging the mining rights and legality to operate on behalf of the local community.

KIRSTEN: there's nothing about growth and development, it benefits a few individuals, but it destroys thousands and thousands and thousands of lives.

VO: She explains that while some hold out for what they consider fair compensation, others are getting impatient.

KIRSTEN: the families that are not agreeing to move have got the pressure from the rest of the families that have signed because they're not going to get paid until those everyone is signed.

VO: Tendele Coal’s Community Development Manager, Nathi Kunene confirmed that no compensation payments have been made to any of the 145 families yet.

NATHI: the truth is, when not all families have signed, you are not certain that you will still have a mine. // we cannot pay those who have signed until everyone signs.

VO: It appears the community is turning on each other.

THABO: We’ve been told those who does not want to move, they are going to be killed.

VO: A spate of violence in the area surrounding the Somkhele mine started in April this year. Sabelo Dladla was a member of the MCEJO sub-committee. He was the first to be targeted.

SABELO: I was visited by two gunmen in my homestead. // it was absolutely a frightening experience to be attacked in your own homestead where you feel safe.

VO: Then, just weeks later, 19 bullets were fired at the home of another anti-mining activist.

KIRSTEN: literally, the bullets came straight through the glass window, through the cupboard that she was standing next to.

VO: 63 year old Fikile Ntshangase was the next target. She was also a member of the sub-committee. Six shots. The final one in the back of her head.

KIRSTEN: they'll stop at nothing.
DEREK: Who do you think they are,
KIRSTEN: the people that want this mine to expand into this new area.

VO: People want to the compensation they’ve been promised.

DEREK: Question?
NATHI: I would say without any fear or doubt, no people have been targeted by the mine // we continue to negotiate because we have to find common ground.

VO: While the perpatrators are still unknown, the cases are under investigation.

Leading up to Ntshangase shooting it seemed that the subcommittee had a change of heart.

After some members met with the mine - there was a memorandum drawn up that the legal cases against the mine would be withdrawn.

SABELO: I changed my mind, one because of the threat, and two, because of the mine has agreed to go to mediation so that all the concerns that have been accumulated for years should be resolved

VO: Fikile Ntshangase was one of two members who did not sign - she was not convinced that this would resolve all their issues with the mining operation.

KIRSTEN: everybody's feeling very fragile and very afraid that the levels of trust in the community, nobody really knows who to trust.//

VO: Youens believes the communication from the mine is not helping these fractures within the community.

In February 2020 the mine stated in a management briefing that “a small amount of households are holding at ransom the mine, its employees, its contractors and all of the families that have already signed contracts.”

DEREK: It's a threat.
NATHI: one may choose to look at it as a threat, but you can imagine if the mine would just close and people had no idea of what is happening and that will impact their lives. So we have a responsibility to communicate.
DEREK: So subtle, that subtle persuasion, is it not?
NATHI: Exactly. I wouldn't call it I wouldn't call it persuasion, but I would call it communication, keeping the community informed.

VO: Environmental Justice Organiser, Bobby Peek, believes Ntshangase’s murder is no coincidence - on average four land and environmental rights defenders are killed each week across the world.

BOBBY: the global reality that we face today shows that people who say no to bad developments, developments that will extract wealth for a few, those people are dying.

VO: Ntshangase was not one of the families identified to move - she was most concerned about families like hers who would be left behind.

LINK: To the left is community of Ophondweni that the mine wants to relocate, to the right is where families will be able to stay – but they will be affected by the impact of the mining operations.

BOBBY: People are living amongst dust, coal dust, coal dust, which will harm you, which will impact upon you negatively. And it's been proven for years. It is not anything new that we have to prove again. So that's the environmental impact. People's lands are put straight and people's health has been destroyed.

SABELO: All we wanted to do was to get a fair compensation from the mine for the people that are surrounding the mine because the mine is already here and it's mining.

VO: According YOUENS, The problem is that the priority for the mine is usually those families in the way of the expansion - not on the borders of it.

KIRSTEN: you're the ones that are most affected, so we'll deal with you. But all of you know, you not actually.
DEREKL Could the mine afford to do that?
KIRSTEN: No, probably not. But then you shouldn't be mining. Do it properly or don't do it at all, comply with the law, do it ethically, morally, speak to the people, negotiate well.

VO: In terms of compensation, Kunene says the mine is in constant negotiations with the affected parties, and that they are using a compensation strategy that is market related.

DEREK: do you think they are holding out for too much money,
NATHI: IN the main, I would say some families are requesting quite too much considering the market related// We've got families that own, say, a three roomed house who demand 10 million,
DEREK: 10 million?
NATHI: 10 million. And that, in our view, is not market related.

VO: BUt Refusing to move won’t stop the mine from coming either.

LINK: The Sangweni’s families moved here since in 1963 it was a peaceful life until 2006 when suddenly the fence was erected and they got new neighbours.

SIFISO: Too much dust. Day and night, SWC, I mean, noise, day and night you can't hang t the washing when the wind is coming to my house. //
DEREK: The water?
SIFISO: The water, even in the tanks, dark.

VO: Sifiso Sangweni’s property is just a few meters away from the mine. He says he was offered R450 000 - for Sifiso it’s just not enough to uproot his family heritage, and start again.

SIFISO: if you ask them how you came to that money. They don't like to talk, they say differently. If you don't want to move, we live here.

VO: While the mine is in relocation negotiations with the Sangweni Family, Kunene claims everything is environmentally above board.

NATHI: in terms of the legislation, the dust levels within the expected limit.

VO: As is the case with all mine operations insisted Kunene.

NATHI: there is proper legislation in place to ensure that mines are regulated and to ensure that mines do comply are inspections which are done. That also applies to our mine. We comply with the legislation.

KIRSTEN: for every expert that shows the way they complying with the law. We've got others that say I'm not?

BOBBY: // I'm not a scientist, but I know when the wind is a stone wall coming towards my house, that the regulations are not saying that that is allowed when my water's running out in my community because the mine has destroyed the geology of the water. I know there's a problem // I don't need the law to tell me there's a problem. But the law, even if it does say it's a problem, the laws do nothing about it








PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: A coal-mine pushing expansion in an environmentally sensitive area. An activist gunned down. We visit a divided community in northern KZN as tension mounts and blood is drawn.

PROMO 2
VO: The expansion of an anthracite mine in northern KwaZulu Natal has brought friction, intimidation and murder to a fractured community torn between those for and against the mining operations.

PROMO 3
VO: An Environmental Justice Activist who fiercely opposed the mining operations in her rural village in KZN - was gunned down in cold blood. We investigate the driving forces dividing a once peaceful community.

What was once an ordinary village in which community members herded cattle and ploughed their fields has turned into a Wild West. Men walk around with revolvers holstered to their sides in the area in which they grew up and raised their families. In November, The Global Environmental Trust, joined by the Centre for Environmental Rights and Mcejo, appeared in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein to try to overturn the 2018 Pietermaritzburg high court ruling that refused to interdict the expansion of Tendele’s operations, which currently cover more than 22 000 hectares. Judgment in the appeal has been reserved. We speak to the affected community members, their legal counsel, the commity and Conservationist Bobby Peek – about the impact, the challenges and the way forward in wa world where activists are increasingly in the firing line.
